extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature; dramatists and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance on how plot (action) and character function in tragedy and drama, including what makes action dramatic, the relation between character and plot, and the aesthetic principle of idealisation in poetic representation. Useful for analysing or composing plays with proper dramatic structure and characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as the first principle / 'soul' of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The plot is the first principle, and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy.’ The plot is the animating principle of the play, the origin of movement, the starting-point and basis of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot must give the play its inner meaning and reality, contain reversals of the situation (περιπέτειαι) and decisive moments that awaken tragic feeling, and realise the intention of the play by converging on a determined end. Without plot, the play could not exist; it is the framework through which character gains dramatic significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must be dramatic (development, results, motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Action, to be dramatic, must be exhibited in its development and in its results; it must stand in reciprocal and causal relation to certain mental states. 'The drama, therefore, is will or emotion in action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the feelings and motives out of which deeds grow and trace the effect of deeds upon the doer's mind. Actions should be motivated and should produce consequences that feed back into further action; isolated deeds lacking development are not dramatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and organic causality of the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic action forms a complete whole: a coherent series of events in organic relation, bound by the law of cause and effect, with an internal centre or pivot (the plot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the play so that incidents and characters are grouped around a central action leading to an appointed end; each part should grow and group itself out of the central nucleus (plot) and contribute causally to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character must be revealed through and shaped by action
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are dramatic only so far as they are grouped round the plot and work in with the movement of events towards an appointed end. The significance of characters arises from their place in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal personality through deeds, choices, collisions with circumstances and other wills. Characters need not be exhaustively depicted in full; they should display those traits necessary for their role in the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic conflict is essential and must manifest outwardly
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama implies a conflict — a collision of forces (external necessity, divided wills, struggles with other human wills) — and 'the dramatic conflict, not the mere plot, is the soul of a tragedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure conflicts have outward manifestations (individual acts, concrete relations) that bring agents into collision with other personalities. Purely inward, solitary mental struggles are not dramatic unless externalised within a plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic character should possess will, energy, and agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic characters should have vital and spontaneous force that can make and mould circumstances: 'It is of the battling, energetic type.' Emotions must harden into will and express themselves in deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor active, resistant personalities who originate action; avoid characters who are merely passive or merely lyrical in emotion. Exceptions (e.g., Hamlet's strenuous inaction) can function as dramatic devices if the inactivity itself operates as a form of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should not be mere complication or puzzle
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is not obliged to be complicated; dramatic complication for its own sake is a defect. Greek tragedy often valued singular, simple structure rather than tangled skeins of incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived mechanism intended only to excite curiosity. Complication is justified only when it serves deeper artistic purposes and the unity and meaning of the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech and dialogue count as action when they propel incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle may have contrasted the man revealed in action with speech that contributes to the march of incident; speech that advances the action counts as action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue and speeches as steps in the action when they express will and change the course of events; avoid monologues or conversational passages that merely emphasize type without advancing the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay: action springs from character and reflects character
rubrics_metrics.description: Where action grows out of character and reflects character, the dramatic conditions are best satisfied: 'The action is the product of the characters and of the circumstances in which they are placed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design actions that plausibly follow from characters' dispositions; make outer events appear as the consequences of inner character (the fate of the hero as his own self recoiling). Maintain a strong bond of probability or necessity binding events together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter and form affect possibility of character development
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of subject-matter (e.g., consecrated legend, epic material) can limit or expand the dramatist's freedom to develop character because audience knowledge and traditional outlines constrain surprises and endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with inherited myths or fixed material, accept limits on modification of main outlines; to explore fuller character development, choose subjects that allow more freedom of invention and background exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern drama: scope for inward life and character-growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern drama opens a richer and more varied inner life and often traces character in growth across a broader time-span, including antecedent circumstances outside the immediate action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In modern plays it is legitimate to show characters' development step by step, expand the temporal canvas, and place more emphasis on subjective motives — but this should not nullify dramatic unity; plot remains artistically primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reflective psychological analysis that undermines action
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscious analysis of character and motive can mar dramatic effect; reflective, emotional characters who lack the energy of will may produce dramatic biographies rather than true dramas (Goethe example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute introspective analysis for decisive action. Preserve the balance between psychological depth and the need for will-driven deeds that constitute drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation / representation of the universal in art
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'idealise' is to represent an object in its permanent and essential aspects, removing transient and accidental features so that the particular broadens into the universal: 'the ideal is the universal' of the Poetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to depict characters and situations that reveal universal human types and truths. Idealisation can heighten beauty and significance; it does not require perfection, but the emphasis of commanding qualities while retaining a plausible human balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's subject-matter differs from tragic idealisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy concerns itself with follies, foibles and imperfections of mankind; because its focus is on flaws and flaws' comic treatment, its mode of generalising differs from tragic idealisation of noble types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or evaluating comedy, expect generalisation through exposure of common faults and exaggeration of foibles rather than the heroic idealisation proper to tragedy; the comic 'ideal' operates by highlighting and universalising defects.
